proposals.relationship: Higginbotham uses Barthes’s account of myth and metalanguage to explain race’s power to organize and obscure other social relations.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1992:254–255/notes 10–11 quotes Mythologies and uses its conceptual vocabulary to explain race as an ideological fact with real effects, neither natural biological essence nor a harmless illusion. Her specific race/gender/class argument remains her own adaptation. The cited Annette Lavers translation (1972), pages 114–115,118,120, was not independently read, and no first-publication claim is inferred from that translation date.

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham uses Althusser’s ideological state apparatuses to explain institutions’ production of racialized gender and class meanings.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 254/note 9 names schools, family, welfare agencies, hospitals and media while explaining how socially constructed gender and class acquire racialized normative meanings. This particular explanatory use coexists with separately credited Foucault, not exclusive derivation or blanket Althusserian affiliation. The cited Ben Brewster translation in Lenin and Philosophy (1972),165 is not newly read.
primary_locators: Signs 17:2 (1992), printed 254, second paragraph and note 9

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham uses Du Bois’s account of divided subjectivity when explaining race as both imposed classification and a language of collective resistance.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 267/note 47 explicitly invokes Du Bois’s 1903 two-ness alongside the collective nation-within-a-nation formulation, retaining Martin Delany’s separate credit. Earlier 252/note 3 also locates anti-biological racial analysis in Du Bois’s work. This is specific conceptual/historical use, not a claim she uncritically adopted every Du Bois racial formulation. Her separate discussion of the 1897 Conservation of Races remains qualified. The cited Souls manifestation is 1970; the original is not newly read.
primary_locators: Signs 17:2 (1992), printed 267/note 47, with 252/note 3 as earlier context

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham places Du Bois’s 1897 racial-spiritual uniqueness within her critical account of romantic racialism and essentialized Black national culture.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 269/note 55, continuing 270, identifies Conservation of Races as an example of the spiritual special-gift conception, then distinguishes the liberating intent of cultural self-recovery from its obscuring of Black heterogeneity. Her critical analytic target is the specific 1897 formulation and a broader racial-national tradition, not all of Du Bois’s changing work or a denial of its anti-racist aims. Fredrickson’s romantic-racialism terminology and Appiah’s separately cited criticism retain credit; original Du Bois/Appiah works unread. Her positive double-consciousness resource remains separate.
primary_locators: Signs 17:2 (1992), printed 269/note 55 through 270, paragraphs on romantic racialism and heterogeneous national culture

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham uses Anderson’s imagined-community framework to situate racialized national belonging as constructed rather than natural.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 268–269/note 52 moves from the forging of a common African diasporic ancestry to non-unique national imaginings and explicitly cites Anderson’s limited, sovereign community. This bounded supporting resource is not proof Anderson originated all Black nationalist thought or that she endorsed biological racial nationalism. The original 1983 book,14–16, remains unread; the cited edition is not replaced with a later revision.

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham uses Williams’s account of language as continual creation to support her analysis of racial language appropriated for resistance.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 270/note 57 cites Marxism and Literature,31, at the point where she explains Black appropriation of productive linguistic power. Bakhtin’s double-voiced discourse and Fanon’s cultural self-recovery retain their separate roles. This particular conceptual support does not establish complete adoption of cultural materialism; original 1977 book unread.
primary_locators: Signs 17:2 (1992), printed 270, first paragraph and note 57

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham uses Cott’s history of passionlessness as a specific counterpoint when distinguishing racialized representations of women’s sexuality.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 263/note 33 names Cott’s analysis of evangelical Protestantism and later science in producing passionlessness for northern white women. The main paragraph contrasts changing white sexual ideals with persistent racist sexualization of Black women, alongside separately credited Laqueur, Jordan and Gilman. This is a bounded historiographic resource, not a claim Cott’s entire work ignored race or a new personal formative influence. Original Cott essay unread.
primary_locators: Signs 17:2 (1992), printed 263, paragraph beginning “In the centuries” and note 33

proposals.relationship: Higginbotham values Kelley’s analysis of violence and imprisonment as a resource for showing how her metalanguage framework illuminates the carceral turn in Black women’s history.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2017:635 explicitly calls Kelley’s historiographic discussion particularly valuable for that specific task, following the introduction’s description at 628–629. This is scholarly uptake in her later forum response, not a causal source of her 1992 article. LeFlouria, Muhammad and the other historians she discusses retain separate credit. Kelley’s complete original forum essay is not newly read. Her bibliography prints a discrepant 509–600; publisher metadata verifies the original article as Signs 42:3,590–600, DOI 10.1086/689623, without silently treating the printed typo as the correct range.
primary_locators: Signs 42:3 (2017), printed 635, second paragraph, with 628–629 introduction and publisher metadata for Kelley’s separate essay
